text:
Yes—within limits, a person should have a qualified right to be forgotten. True information is not automatically public property forever, and a decent society should recognize that people can change. In the case of someone convicted of a serious offence twenty years ago who has not reoffended, the strongest position is that the information should not be erased from history, but it may justifiably be removed from easy public access in many contexts.

The key distinction is between deletion and obscurity. A right to be forgotten should not mean rewriting the past, destroying court records, or pretending the offence never happened. It should mean limiting the indefinite, algorithm-driven circulation of old information when its continued prominence serves little public interest and causes disproportionate harm. Before the internet, time itself created practical obscurity: old newspaper reports existed, but they did not instantly define someone’s life every time an employer, neighbour, or stranger searched their name. Digital archives and search engines have destroyed that obscurity. A punishment that was once finite can become effectively permanent.

That matters morally. Criminal punishment is supposed to have limits. If a person has served their sentence and then lived lawfully for twenty years, continuing to make the offence the first fact anyone learns about them undermines rehabilitation. It can block employment, housing, relationships, and participation in civic life. In effect, society keeps punishing the person long after the courts have finished. If we believe in reform, we must leave room for people to re-enter society as more than the worst thing they have done.

There are also practical reasons for this view. Stable reintegration reduces the risk of future offending. People with jobs, housing, and social ties are less likely to relapse into crime. A legal system that says “debt paid” while the internet says “sentence never ends” is self-defeating. Public shaming may satisfy curiosity, but it does not necessarily improve public safety.

Still, this right cannot be absolute, especially in serious cases. The public sometimes has a legitimate interest in knowing about past wrongdoing. If the person seeks a position of trust—working with children, entering politics, practicing medicine, managing clients’ money—old convictions may remain relevant. Journalistic archives also have value, and victims’ experiences should not be erased for the convenience of offenders. There is an important difference between removing a search result for a name-based query and forcing a newspaper to delete a lawful article from its archive. The former reduces casual exposure; the latter risks censorship and damage to the historical record.

So in the case of a serious offence from twenty years ago with no reoffending, I would argue for limited delisting rather than total removal. Search engines should, in many cases, stop surfacing old reports when someone searches the person’s name, unless there is a continuing public-interest reason. Original court and news records could remain accessible through archives, legal databases, or more specific searches. Employers or authorities in specially regulated fields could still obtain relevant background information through lawful channels. This approach balances rehabilitation, privacy, public safety, and freedom of information.

The strongest objection is that truth should always remain accessible, and that restricting access invites censorship. But unrestricted accessibility is not the same as freedom. Search engines do not merely reflect reality; they rank and amplify it. Choosing not to make a decades-old conviction the top result for every name search is not the same as lying. It is a judgment that relevance changes over time.

In short, a person should have a right to be forgotten in the sense of a right not to be endlessly and automatically defined by old, true, damaging information. For someone convicted of a serious offence twenty years ago who has not reoffended, society should preserve the historical record but reduce its routine public visibility. Justice should include the possibility that, after enough time and genuine reform, a person can live in the present rather than forever under the shadow of the past.
